title: 📘 UNIT 7: STATES, PRINCIPALITIES, POPULATION MOVEMENTS AND INTERACTIONS IN ETHIOPIA (13TH–MID-16TH CENTURY)
notes:
Period → 1270 to mid-16th century.

Main developments → restoration of the Solomonic Dynasty + growth of Muslim sultanates + expansion of the Christian highland kingdom + Zeyla trade + Adal-Christian conflicts + Oromo population movement.

📌 Major forces shaping the period → trade, religion, territorial expansion, warfare, migration and political interaction.

title: 7.1 👑 The Christian Highland Kingdom under the Restored Solomonic Dynasty
notes:
1270 → Yikuno Amlak overthrew the Zagwe Dynasty and established the restored 'Solomonic' Dynasty.

👑 Yikuno Amlak (r.1270–1285) → claimed descent from the ancient Aksumite royal line through Dil Naod and used the Queen of Sheba–King Solomon tradition to establish political legitimacy.

📖 Kibre Negest → 14th-century work that preserved the Solomonic tradition.

🏛️ Capital → initially shifted from Lalibela toward Lake Hayk and later toward Shewa; moving/roving capitals became characteristic.

📌 The dynasty continued for more than 700 years, until 1974.

title: 7.1.1 🏰 State Structure, Society and Economy
notes:
Territorial expansion → became especially rapid under King Amde Tsiyon.

⛪ Christianity → expanded together with the kingdom into Shewa, Gojjam, Begemdir and Lake Tana areas.

🌾 Economy → agriculture was the main foundation; mixed farming was widespread.

💰 Trade → Zeyla became the major gateway for internal and external trade between 1270–1529.

Major trade goods → ivory, gold, cereals and other agricultural products.

Muslim merchants → dominated much of the Zeyla trade.

📌 Trade created economic interdependence but competition for control of trade routes caused repeated conflicts.

title: 7.1.2 ⚔️ Gult and Rist Systems
notes:
Rist → hereditary right to use land by members of families or clans whose ancestors had long possessed it.

Gult → right to collect tribute from holders of rist land and its produce.

👤 Bale Gult → holder of gult rights.

Main duties → collect tribute + maintain law and order + administer justice + raise regional armies + provide military service.

Tribute could include → grain, cattle, honey, butter, salt and household goods.

📌 Gult became a major feature of Ethiopian feudalism and remained important until the 1974 Revolution.

title: 7.1.3 🔄 Moving Capitals and Succession
notes:
1270–1636 → no permanent capital in the Christian highland kingdom.

Royal court → moved between districts of Shewa with soldiers, officials and camp followers.

Reasons for movement → obtain food and supplies + shortage of firewood + suppress rebellions + maintain control.

👑 Zer'a Ya'ekob (r.1434–1468) → founded Debre Birhan in 1454 and stayed there for about 14 years.

Succession crisis → after Yikuno Amlak, rivalry among royal descendants caused instability.

1294–1299 → five kings briefly succeeded one another.

⛰️ Amba Gishen/Debre Negest → established around 1300 to keep male royal descendants away from political competition.

📌 The system helped stabilize royal succession until Amba Gishen was destroyed by Imam Ahmad in 1540.

title: 7.1.4 ⚔️ Amde Tsiyon and Territorial Expansion
notes:
👑 Amde Tsiyon (r.1314–1344) → the most expansionist king of the medieval period.

Major conquests →
• Damot → 1316/17.
• Gojjam → 1323/24.
• Felasha → 1332.
• Northern territories → expanded toward Massawa.

🏷️ Ma'ikele Bahr → title of the governor appointed in the Red Sea coastal region.

Amde Tsiyon also defeated Ifat and other Muslim sultanates, reducing many to tributary status.

📌 Expansion provided manpower, tribute and access to trade resources.

title: 7.1.5 ☪️ Christian Kingdom vs Muslim Sultanates
notes:
Main cause of rivalry → competition over Zeyla trade, trade routes and control of territories.

Ifat → the strongest Muslim sultanate; challenged Christian control of trade routes.

1332 → Ifat was defeated and became tributary to the Christian kingdom.

Walasma rulers → later moved east and established Adal around 1380.

⚔️ Adal became the major new challenger to the Christian highland kingdom.

1445 → King Zer'a Ya'ekob defeated Sultan Ahmad Badlay, marking the peak of Christian political dominance in the region.

Late 15th century → Christian power declined, while Adal grew stronger.

title: 7.1.6 ⛪ Religious Expansion and Church-State Relations
notes:
Christian territorial expansion → accompanied by expansion of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church.

⛪ Debre Asbo → founded by Abune Tekle Haymanot; later became Debre Libanos.

⛪ Hayk Istifanos → monastery associated with Abba Iyasus Mo'a.

Christianity spread → Shewa + Gojjam + Damot + Ennarya + Wajj and other regions.

Church-state alliance → kings supported churches and monasteries with land and resources; clergy supported Christian teaching and the legitimacy of the kings.

👑 Zer'a Ya'ekob → church-state relationship reached a high point during his reign.

title: 7.2 ☪️ Expansion of Islam and Muslim Sultanates
notes:
Main factors in the rise of Muslim sultanates → Islam + long-distance trade.

Main routes of Islamic expansion → Red Sea coast + Zeyla/Gulf of Aden.

📍 Zeyla → most important gateway for Islam into the interior.

👥 Muslim merchants → established markets along trade routes and helped spread Islam peacefully through commercial and social interaction.

Major Sultanates → Shewa, Ifat, Fatagar, Dawaro, Darha, Bali, Hadya, Arababni, Sharkha and Adal.

Common features → Muslim populations + rulers with political and religious authority + trade-based economies + concentration mainly in southeastern lowlands.

title: 7.2.1 🛍️ Zeyla Trade and Trade Routes
notes:
Zeyla → most important trade outlet during the medieval period.

Other ports → Mogadishu + Brava + Merca + Massawa.

Trade routes → connected the interior with coastal markets and the wider Red Sea/Arabian world.

Major effects →
• Growth of towns and markets.
• Rise and consolidation of Muslim sultanates.
• Economic interdependence among peoples.
• Exchange of cultural and social values.
• Increased rivalry over control of trade.

📌 Zeyla trade was both a source of cooperation and a major cause of political conflict.

title: 7.2.2 🕌 Important Muslim Sultanates
notes:
🏛️ IFAT → emerged around the mid-13th century; Umar Walasma was its first historically known ruler. Walasma dynasty ruled Ifat. Strategic position along Zeyla routes made it powerful.

🏛️ HADYA → westernmost major Muslim sultanate; rulers used the title Garad. Economy → mixed farming + pastoralism + trade. Often rebelled against Christian rule.

🏛️ BALI → southernmost sultanate; rulers used Garad. Paid tribute to the Christian highland kingdom until the 16th century.

🏛️ SHARKHA → small sultanate roughly corresponding to present-day Arsi; became tributary to the Christian kingdom.

🏛️ DAWARO → located south of Fatagar; included groups of Oromo and ancestors of Sidama peoples.

🏛️ DARHA → small sultanate east of the Awash between Dawaro and Bali.

🏛️ FATAGAR → emerged along the Zeyla route; later became a province directly ruled by the Christian kingdom.

🏛️ ARABABNI → small sultanate south of the Awash between Hadya and Dawaro.

🏛️ ADAL → founded by Walasma rulers around 1380 after retreating from Ifat; centered first at Dakar and later Harar.

title: 7.3 🌍 Southern, Western and Central States
notes:
Alongside the Christian kingdom and Muslim sultanates, many indigenous states existed in southern, western and central Ethiopia.

Major examples → Gojjam + Bizamo + Wajj + Ganz + Ennarya + Gonga states.

Most communities → practiced indigenous religions and developed their own political and social institutions.

📌 These states were important in agriculture, trade, cultural exchange and regional politics.

title: 7.3.1 🌿 Gojjam, Bizamo, Wajj and Ganz
notes:
🏞️ Gojjam → south of Lake Tana; mainly inhabited by Agew. Reduced to tributary status by Amde Tsiyon around 1323/24.

👑 Zhan Kimir → ruler of Gojjam during Amde Tsiyon's reign.

🏞️ Bizamo → south of the Abay River; inhabited by Omotic speakers including Shinasha. Became tributary to the Christian kingdom.

🏞️ Wajj → around Lake Ziway; rulers used the Muslim title Qats. Later occupied by Oromo groups.

🏞️ Ganz → probably in the Rift Valley between Wajj, Kambata and Hadya; rulers used the title Garad.

title: 7.3.2 🏺 Ennarya and the Gonga Peoples
notes:
🏞️ Ennarya → located north of the Gojeb River and west of the upper Gibe River.

Economy → important source of trade goods, especially gold.

💰 Gold from Ennarya → exported as far as Egypt, Greece and Rome.

Gonga peoples → speakers of Kafi Noonoo, Shekki Noonoo, Anfillo, Shinasha, Ennarya and Bosha languages.

Major Gonga states → Ennarya + Anfillo + Bizamo + Kafa + Shekka.

👑 Kafa and Shekka rulers → used the title Tato.

🛡️ Defense → trenches, stone fortifications and enclosures were built to protect their territories.

title: 7.4 ⚔️ Christian Highland Kingdom vs Sultanate of Adal (1520s–1559)
notes:
Adal experienced internal political rivalry during the late 15th century.

👤 Emir Mahfuz → strengthened Adal and attacked the Christian kingdom; killed at Zeyla in 1517.

👤 Imam Ahmad ibn-Ibrahim al-Ghazi → popularly called Gragn ('left-handed'); became the dominant leader of Adal in the early 1520s.

Main objective → restore Adal's independence + control Zeyla trade + establish a powerful Islamic empire.

📌 The conflict was strongly connected to political, economic and territorial rivalry, especially control of trade routes.

title: 7.4.1 ⚔️ Imam Ahmad's Campaigns
notes:
1527 → Imam Ahmad began major attacks against Christian tributary territories.

1529 → Battle of Shimbra Kure → Imam Ahmad defeated King Libne Dingil's army.

1531 → Dawaro and Bali were annexed.

1532–1533 → Adal controlled much of southern Ethiopia.

1533–1535 → Imam Ahmad expanded into northern provinces and made Aksum an important center.

1535 → Dembiya near Lake Tana became his command center.

⚔️ Wolaita → the major southern state that successfully resisted Imam Ahmad's forces.

📌 Adal temporarily became the dominant power in the Ethiopian region and much of the Horn.

title: 7.4.2 🇵🇹 Ottoman and Portuguese Involvement
notes:
🇵🇹 Portugal → supported the Christian highland kingdom with military assistance.

1541 → about 400 Portuguese soldiers led by Christovao da Gama arrived in Ethiopia.

🇹🇷 Ottoman Empire → supplied Imam Ahmad with soldiers, muskets and cannons.

⚔️ Wefla → Portuguese forces suffered a major defeat; Christovao da Gama was captured and killed.

1543 → Battle of Woyna Dega → combined Ethiopian and Portuguese forces defeated Imam Ahmad.

👤 Imam Ahmad → killed after being shot by a Portuguese musketeer.

📌 Adal's brief supremacy ended, but conflict continued until 1559.

title: 7.4.3 💥 Consequences of the Adal–Christian Wars
notes:
Major consequences →
• Massive loss of human life.
• Destruction of churches and monasteries.
• Loss of religious manuscripts and cultural property.
• Weakening of the Christian highland kingdom.
• Destruction of imperial armies.
• Growth of regional political power.
• Population displacement and migration.
• Increased interaction and mixing of ethnic and religious groups.
• Disruption of Zeyla trade.

📌 The wars weakened central authority and contributed to later political instability.

title: 7.5 🧭 Population Movements in the Ethiopian Region
notes:
Population movement → movement of communities from one settlement area to another due to environmental, economic, political or military pressures.

14th–16th centuries → Somali, Afar and Argoba movements were influenced by warfare, drought, famine, trade and search for pasture.

The largest movement discussed → Oromo population movement beginning on a large scale in the 16th century.

title: 7.5.1 🐪 Somali, Afar and Argoba Movements
notes:
🐪 SOMALI → moved inland from coastal areas including Zeyla, Berbera, Benadir and Mogadishu. During Imam Ahmad's wars, many Somali joined Adal's army. Pastoral groups also moved toward highlands seeking water and pasture.

🐪 AFAR → ancient inhabitants of northeastern Ethiopia, Djibouti and southeastern Eritrea. Drought and famine encouraged movement toward the Middle Awash. During the wars, pastoral groups moved toward safer areas and some supported Imam Ahmad.

🛤️ ARGOBA → early Muslim inhabitants of the region; important agents of trade, Islamic expansion and Muslim state formation. Their location along caravan routes exposed them strongly to war and trade-related movement.

title: 7.5.2 🐎 Oromo Population Movement: Causes
notes:
Large-scale movement → began from the Bale highlands in the early 16th century.

Main causes →
• Growth of cattle population.
• Shortage of pasture in Bale.
• Search for better grazing land.
• Availability of fertile lowlands.
• Wars involving Adal and the Christian kingdom weakened frontier defenses.
• Population pressure and economic needs.

📌 The movement accelerated after the defeat and death of Imam Ahmad.

title: 7.5.3 🗺️ Directions and Stages of Oromo Movement
notes:
Before the major movement → Oromo were organized mainly into two confederacies:

🔵 Borana → Macha + Tulama + Guji + Southern Borana.

🟠 Barantu → Karayu + Ittu + Marawa + Akkachu + Arsi + Humbana.

🔵 Borana direction → central and southwestern Ethiopia; some groups moved toward northern Kenya.

🟠 Barantu direction → northeast toward Awash, Harar, Wollo and surrounding regions.

1522 → Macha and Tulama began major northward movement.

1550s–1580s → rapid expansion into central, southeastern, western, southern and some northern areas.

📍 Odaa Nabee → established as a major center near Dukam in the early 1560s.

title: 7.5.4 🔄 Effects of Oromo Population Movement
notes:
Political effects → several states were destroyed, weakened or incorporated.

Affected states → Hadya + Bali + Sharkha + Dawaro + Fatagar + Wajj + Bizamo + Damot + Gafat and others.

Christian highland kingdom → increasingly restricted to territories north of the Abay River.

Adal → reduced mainly to the walled city of Harar and surrounding area.

👥 Social effects → increased interaction and mixing among Oromo and other peoples.

🤝 Moggassa → groups that accepted Oromo incorporation could become members of an Oromo sub-group and receive social, economic and political rights.

📌 Resistance → communities that resisted could face warfare, loss of property and displacement.

title: 7.5.5 🏛️ Gadaa System
notes:
Gadaa → indigenous democratic socio-political system of the Oromo.

Functions → regulated political + economic + social + religious life.

⏳ Gadaa grades → responsibilities changed in eight-year stages.

Important grades → Dabale (0–8) → Game-Titiko (8–16) → Game-Gurgudo (16–24) → Kusa (24–32) → Raba-Doori (32–40) → Gada (40–48).

🏛️ Chaffee → Gadaa assembly operating at local, regional and central levels.

👤 Abbaa Gadaa/Abbaa Bokku → highest political authority; first among equals.

👤 Abbaa Sera → chief judge.

👤 Abbaa Duulaa → commander of the army.

📌 Officials were elected based on ability, knowledge, oratory, leadership and military experience.

title: 7.5.6 ⚖️ Gadaa Democracy, Siinqee and Decline
notes:
Gadaa government → had executive, legislative and judicial functions that helped balance power.

Buqqisu → removal of corrupt or dictatorial leaders before the end of their term.

👩 Siinqee → parallel institution through which Oromo women's participation and gender equality were expressed; also supported peace-making.

🌿 Gadaa and Oromo expansion → helped organize society, maintain unity and coordinate political and military activities.

Decline factors → rise of powerful Abbaa Duulaa + long-distance trade + spread of Islam + interaction with monarchical states + missionary influence + influence of hierarchical imperial structures.

📌 Eventually, Gadaa became mainly ritual and ceremonial in many areas.

title: 7.5.7 🤝 Moggassa and Guddifacha
notes:
Moggassa → collective adoption of an Oromo or non-Oromo group through an oath ceremony before the Abbaa Gadaa.

Adopted groups → became Ilma Gossa and received social, economic and political rights.

Benefits → increased population + strengthened military power + integrated other communities + provided protection.

Guddifacha → individual adoption; an adopted child was treated as a real son and received the rights of a true son.

📌 These institutions helped the Oromo integrate different peoples during population movement.

title: 🏆 UNIT 7 — MUST REMEMBER
notes:
👑 SOLomonic DYNASTY

1270 → Yikuno Amlak overthrew Zagwe.

Kibre Negest → legitimized Solomonic claim.

Amde Tsiyon → major territorial expansion.

Gult → tribute-collecting right.

Rist → hereditary land-use right.

Amba Gishen → helped solve succession problems.

☪️ MUSLIM SULTANATES

Islam + trade → major factors in their emergence.

Zeyla → main gateway for trade and Islamic expansion.

Ifat → powerful Walasma sultanate.

Adal → founded by Walasma rulers around 1380.

⚔️ ADAL–CHRISTIAN CONFLICT

Imam Ahmad → major leader of Adal.

1529 → Shimbra Kure → Imam Ahmad's victory.

1535 → Adal reached its greatest territorial dominance.

1543 → Woyna Dega → Imam Ahmad defeated and killed.

1559 → Gelawdewos killed; conflict ended.

🐎 OROMO MOVEMENT

Origin → Bale highlands.

Beginning → early 16th century.

Main causes → pasture shortage + cattle growth + wars + search for fertile land.

Borana → central/southwestern direction.

Barantu → northeastern direction.

Odaa Nabee → important assembly center.

🏛️ GADAA
Democratic Oromo socio-political system.

Chaffee → assembly.

Abbaa Gadaa → highest authority.

Abbaa Sera → chief judge.

Abbaa Duulaa → army commander.

Siinqee → women's institution and peace-making.

Moggassa → collective adoption.

Guddifacha → individual adoption.

🧠 EXAM CONNECTION:

Yikuno Amlak → restored Solomonic Dynasty.

Amde Tsiyon → expansion + tributary states.

Zeyla → trade + Islamic expansion + conflict.

Ifat → Walasma dynasty.

Adal → Walasma rulers + Imam Ahmad.

Shimbra Kure → 1529 → Imam Ahmad victory.

Woyna Dega → 1543 → Imam Ahmad defeated.

Gadaa → Oromo democratic governance.

Moggassa → integration/adoption of groups.

Guddifacha → individual adoption.

📌 KEY DATES:

1270 → Yikuno Amlak established Solomonic Dynasty.

c.1300 → Amba Gishen established.

1314–1344 → reign of Amde Tsiyon.

1332 → Ifat defeated and made tributary.

1380 → Adal established.

1445 → Zer'a Ya'ekob defeated Ahmad Badlay.

1517 → Emir Mahfuz killed.

1522 → major Oromo movement began under Macha and Tulama.

1529 → Battle of Shimbra Kure.

1531 → Dawaro and Bali conquered by Imam Ahmad.

1543 → Battle of Woyna Dega; Imam Ahmad killed.

1550s–1580s → rapid Oromo expansion.

1559 → Gelawdewos killed; Adal-Christian conflict ended.
